nodes.name: deploy config (render.yaml)
nodes.raw:
# VitalX — despliegue en Render. La app vive en dashboard/, no en la raiz.
services:
  - type: web
    name: vitalx
    runtime: node
    plan: starter
    region: oregon
    buildCommand: pnpm run build   # delega a dashboard/, funciona sin Root Directory
    startCommand: pnpm run start
    healthCheckPath: /login
    autoDeploy: true
    envVars:
      - key: NODE_VERSION
        value: "22"
      - key: DATABASE_URL
        sync: false          # Neon
      - key: BETTER_AUTH_SECRET
        sync: false
      - key: BETTER_AUTH_URL
        value: https://app.vitalx.dev
      - key: ANTHROPIC_API_KEY
        sync: false          # inferencia con Haiku
      - key: INGEST_DIR
        value: data          # legado del almacenamiento en archivos; ya lee Postgres

  # Landing estatica: HTML plano en landing/, sin build.
  - type: web
    name: vitalx-landing
    runtime: static
    staticPublishPath: ./landing
    autoDeploy: true

nodes.name: build
nodes.raw: "build": "pnpm --dir dashboard install --frozen-lockfile && pnpm --dir dashboard run db:migrate && pnpm --dir dashboard run build"

writeBoundary.producer: Render's build/deploy runner and its HTTP health prober
writeBoundary.argument: This is the only edge in the repo that can block a change from shipping — there is no .github/, no CI, no pre-commit hook. autoDeploy:true sends every push to Render, which runs buildCommand `pnpm run build` in its own builder and then probes healthCheckPath /login over HTTP before cutting traffic. Both signals are emitted outside the repo: the builder's exit code comes from pnpm/drizzle/next processes, and the 200 comes from a request Render originates. It is falsifiable in a way the author cannot suppress: dashboard/instrumentation.ts throws at boot when DATABASE_URL is unset, so a misconfigured deploy dies at the probe. The limit worth naming: this gate asserts only 'it compiled, migrated, booted and served /login' — /login is a static Next page with a Suspense fallback, so the probe carries no claim about application behaviour.

writeBoundary.producer: pnpm's lockfile resolver, drizzle-kit against Neon Postgres, and the TypeScript compiler inside `next build`
writeBoundary.argument: Three chained processes each own their own exit code and each is on Render's deploy path. `pnpm install --frozen-lockfile` fails if pnpm-lock.yaml disagrees with package.json — the resolver, not the author, decides. `db:migrate` submits DDL to a real Postgres that accepts or rejects it. `next build` type-checks the whole app; dashboard/next.config.ts sets only images.unoptimized, so typescript.ignoreBuildErrors stays false and a type error is a nonzero exit. Nothing in the repo can rewrite those verdicts. What it does not assert: any runtime behaviour — this repo has no test runner installed at all.

evidence: package.json build: pnpm --dir dashboard install --frozen-lockfile && ... db:migrate && ... build

writeBoundary.producer: tsc/Next compiler process invoked by `next build`
writeBoundary.argument: Same producer as the root build one level down: the compiler decides, and the compiler is not something dashboard/ code can persuade. Reached on every deploy via root `build`. Its assertion is narrow — well-typed and bundleable — and on the oracle axis it is weak in the usual way: the types were authored by the same hand as the implementation, so the check proves the code agrees with its own annotations.

evidence: invoked by root package.json build, which render.yaml runs

writeBoundary.producer: the Neon Postgres server executing drizzle-kit's migration SQL
writeBoundary.argument: drizzle-kit migrate opens DATABASE_URL and hands SQL to a database the repo does not host. Postgres's parser and constraint engine produce the success/failure, and an unreachable DB or an invalid migration aborts the build before Render starts the service. The signal is about schema applicability only — a migration that applies cleanly says nothing about whether the schema is the right one.

evidence: root build chains db:migrate before next build

writeBoundary.producer: the atc-judge LLM skill, which writes verdict.outcome into the same run JSONs the report then aggregates
writeBoundary.argument: atc-report.mjs computes task attribution purely from `r.verdict.outcome`, and that field is written by .claude/skills/atc-judge/SKILL.md — a Claude skill that reads screenshots and stamps completed/failed/inconclusive into out/<ts>/*.json. The runs themselves are produced by the sibling atc-run skill. So an agent generates the trace and an agent of the same class scores it; the report is arithmetic over that scoring, adding no independent observation. Two mitigations belong in the record and neither changes the class: the judge is a separate pass from the executor, and it is explicitly instructed to ignore the executor's `agent_reported` narration and read screenshots instead. Correlated blind spots survive both. Nothing invokes `report` automatically either — it is an operator command.

writeBoundary.producer: the eslint process (next/core-web-vitals config) — but no traceable consumer
writeBoundary.argument: The fork point on the producer side is clear: eslint exits nonzero on its own findings. What I cannot establish is whether this edge exists at all. There is no .github/workflows, no husky or .git hooks config, no pre-commit file, and Next 16's `next build` no longer runs ESLint, so nothing in the deploy path consults it. That leaves a command a human may or may not have run before pushing — a lint file rather than a lint check. I am declining to call it not_a_check, because it is genuinely capable of failing when run; the untraceable part is whether anything reads it, and that is what unknown is for.

evidence: no .github, no hook config anywhere in repo
next 16.2.7 in dependencies (build no longer lints)

writeBoundary.argument: A launcher. It delegates to `next start` and asserts nothing about correctness — the process either serves or it does not, and the assertion about that lives one edge away in Render's health probe, which is where I classified it. Counting this separately would double-count the same signal.

evidence: package.json start: pnpm --dir dashboard run start

writeBoundary.argument: `next start` produces a running service, not a verdict. Nothing about its invocation distinguishes a correct build from an incorrect one.
A local development server. It is never run by any pipeline and emits no pass/fail signal about the codebase.

Filesystem plumbing that runs on the deploy path but is deliberately built not to fail: link-out.mjs comments that out/ is gitignored and therefore absent on a clean Render deploy, and exits successfully when there is nothing to link. A step engineered to succeed regardless of the state of the code cannot carry information about the code.

evidence: dashboard/package.json prebuild: node scripts/link-out.mjs && node scripts/link-probe.mjs
dashboard/scripts/link-out.mjs: 'sin la carpeta simplemente no hay nada que enlazar y el build debe seguir'

writeBoundary.producer: node running the same two symlink scripts
writeBoundary.argument: Identical plumbing to prebuild, on the local dev path instead of the deploy path. Creates symlinks; asserts nothing.

evidence: dashboard/package.json predev: node scripts/link-out.mjs && node scripts/link-probe.mjs

writeBoundary.argument: Emits migration SQL from the schema file. It is an authoring step whose output is committed and later executed by db:migrate — the verdict-bearing edge is that execution against Postgres, not this generation.
